extracted.intended_audience: beginners interested in learning improvisational theater / new improvisers
extracted.subtask_description: A practical how-to guide for people new to improvisational theater, covering core principles, class selection, exercises, stage-fright management, first-performance prep, ongoing practice, and common improv formats.

rubrics_metrics.name: Say "Yes, And..."
rubrics_metrics.description: This is the cornerstone of improv. Always accept what your partner offers ("yes") and then add something new ("and").
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintains momentum and builds trust. Example: If someone says "Look at that giant chicken," respond with "Yes! And it’s about to cross the road."

rubrics_metrics.name: Listen Actively
rubrics_metrics.description: Good improvisers listen intently instead of planning their next line while someone else talks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Active listening helps you respond authentically and keep scenes grounded in what has just happened.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid Blocking
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not reject or negate ideas from another performer; blocking kills the scene.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anti-patterns: saying "That’s stupid" or "No that can’t happen." Such responses stop flow and damage collaborative momentum.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make Your Partner Look Good
rubrics_metrics.description: Improv is collaborative — help fellow performers shine instead of trying to take control.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Support teammates’ ideas, add details that reinforce their choices, and avoid dominating scenes to be the 'star.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Stay Present
rubrics_metrics.description: Focus fully on what is happening right now in the scene rather than worrying about mistakes or future lines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Being present improves responsiveness and makes scenes feel real. Mind-wandering or pre-planning weakens the connection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Embrace Mistakes
rubrics_metrics.description: There are no mistakes in improv — only opportunities to adapt creatively.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mistakes can lead to unexpected humor or story twists; treat errors as material to build on rather than failures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose a Class Labeled 'Introductory' or 'Beginner'
rubrics_metrics.description: For beginners, look for classes specifically labeled 'introductory' or 'beginner.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Beginner classes provide structured warm-ups and fundamentals geared to newcomers rather than advanced techniques.

rubrics_metrics.name: Check Teaching Style (comedy vs. storytelling)
rubrics_metrics.description: Investigate whether a class emphasizes comedy or storytelling — instructors vary in focus.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pick a teaching style that matches your goals (e.g., comedic short-form games vs. narrative long-form practice).

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider Time Commitment
rubrics_metrics.description: Be aware of time requirements: weekly sessions over several weeks are common for improv classes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose a course whose schedule you can commit to; progress comes from repeated practice rather than one-off lessons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ensure a Welcoming, Non-Judgmental Environment
rubrics_metrics.description: Select classes or groups that feel supportive and non-judgmental for beginners.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A safe practice space encourages risk-taking and learning; vet studios by reading reviews or asking about teaching philosophy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider Online Improv Workshops If No Local Options
rubrics_metrics.description: If in-person classes are unavailable, online improv workshops are a popular alternative.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Online formats can still offer guided warm-ups and scene work; check instructor experience and class interactivity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Name Games (icebreaker)
rubrics_metrics.description: Each person says their name with an adjective starting with the same letter (e.g., 'Jolly John').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Warms up memory, builds group rapport, and creates a friendly atmosphere for beginners.

rubrics_metrics.name: Word Association Exercise
rubrics_metrics.description: Players sit in a circle and quickly say words linked to the previous word.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sharpens spontaneity, rapid connections, and loosens up automatic censoring of odd ideas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Gibberish Talk
rubrics_metrics.description: Performers speak in made-up language while conveying emotion through tone and body language.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Enhances physical expressiveness and the ability to communicate emotion and intent without relying on specific words.

rubrics_metrics.name: Freeze Tag Exercise
rubrics_metrics.description: Two performers start a scene; someone yells 'freeze!' and replaces one performer, starting a new scene inspired by the frozen pose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practices quick thinking, physicality, and deriving scene ideas from physical positions or images.

rubrics_metrics.name: One-Word Story
rubrics_metrics.description: Participants construct a story by contributing one word at a time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Promotes teamwork, listening, and the skill of building coherence from minimal contributions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Start Small to Overcome Stage Fright
rubrics_metrics.description: Begin with low-pressure exercises before participating in full scenes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gradual exposure builds confidence; avoid jumping immediately to high-stakes performance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Focus Outward (not on yourself)
rubrics_metrics.description: Concentrate on your scene partners rather than your own nerves or appearance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Shifting attention away from self reduces self-consciousness and improves responsiveness and connection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Breathe Deeply to Calm Nerves
rubrics_metrics.description: Use controlled breathing techniques to manage anxiety before and during performance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Breathing exercises can reduce physiological arousal and help maintain focus.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accept Imperfection
rubrics_metrics.description: Remind yourself that mistakes are part of learning and improv.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lowering perfectionist pressure encourages risk-taking and makes performances more playful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practice Regularly to Build Confidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Confidence grows with repetition and consistent practice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frequent practice sessions, even short ones, compound into greater stage comfort and responsiveness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Visualize Success
rubrics_metrics.description: Use positive mental imagery to reduce anxiety and prepare for performance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Setting positive expectations can improve actual performance and lower pre-show nerves.

rubrics_metrics.name: Get Plenty of Rest Before Performances
rubrics_metrics.description: Prioritize sleep and rest rather than intensive last-minute preparation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Being well-rested supports clearer thinking, faster recall, and better physical performance on stage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Warm Up Physically Before Performing
rubrics_metrics.description: Do physical stretches and warm-ups to prepare your body for stage work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Physical warm-ups loosen tension, improve vocal projection, and make movement choices easier and safer.

rubrics_metrics.name: Arrive Early to Observe
rubrics_metrics.description: Get to the venue early so you can watch others and acclimate to the space.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Observing helps reduce anxiety, gives context for the audience and format, and provides inspiration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Set an Intention for Your Performance
rubrics_metrics.description: Choose a simple intention like 'I will say yes' or 'I will support my team' before going on stage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Intentions provide focus and a concrete guideline to fall back on during uncertainty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bring Water and Dress Comfortably
rubrics_metrics.description: Practical prep: stay hydrated and wear comfortable clothing appropriate for movement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comfort reduces distractions and lets you concentrate on performance rather than physical discomfort.

rubrics_metrics.name: Watch Improv Shows to Learn
rubrics_metrics.description: View professional improvisers to gain inspiration and learn about different formats and pacing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Watching helps you internalize structure, comic timing, and choices used in short-form and long-form shows.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practice Daily Brainstorming
rubrics_metrics.description: Generate unusual or many ideas daily to keep creativity fluid.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Habitual idea generation makes it easier to find interesting offers and details on stage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Join an Improv Troupe When Ready
rubrics_metrics.description: Audition for or join a local troupe once comfortable with basics and regular practice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Troupe membership provides consistent rehearsal, performance opportunities, and collaborative growth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Read Foundational Books on Improv
rubrics_metrics.description: Study texts such as Truth in Comedy and Impro to deepen understanding of theory and technique.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reading supplements practice by explaining concepts, history, and advanced frameworks to apply on stage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Record Yourself Performing
rubrics_metrics.description: Film or audio-record scenes to review strengths and areas for improvement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Self-review helps identify habits, slack moments, and opportunities for clearer choices and funnier beats.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize Short-Form Formats
rubrics_metrics.description: Short-form consists of quick games lasting 1–5 minutes, often comedic (e.g., 'Props,' 'Scenes from a Hat').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Short-form emphasizes fast payoffs, tight premises, and quick character choices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize Long-Form Formats
rubrics_metrics.description: Long-form involves extended scenes developed from one suggestion that can evolve into interconnected stories (e.g., The Harold).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Long-form requires sustained listening, pattern recognition, and the ability to develop callbacks and relationships.

rubrics_metrics.name: Musical Improv
rubrics_metrics.description: Scenes created spontaneously with singing and musical structure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Requires additional skills in melody, rhythm, and integrating sung material with improvised narrative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Themed Shows
rubrics_metrics.description: Shows based on specific genres or audience suggestions (e.g., sci-fi night).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Themed formats provide constraints that can inspire creative choices and a coherent evening of scenes.
